hits: Conjecture: Each positive integer n can be written as a_1 + ... + a_k, where a_1,...,a_k are strict partition numbers (i.e., terms of the current sequence) with no one dividing another. This has been verified for n = 1..1350. - _Zhi-Wei Sun_, Apr 14 2023

Conjecture: For each integer n > 7, a(n) divides none of p(n), p(n) - 1 and p(n) + 1, where p(n) is the number of partitions of n given by A000041. This has been verified for n up to 10^5. - _Zhi-Wei Sun_, May 20 2023 [Verified for n <= 2*10^6. - _Vaclav Kotesovec_, May 23 2023]
A000009.name: Expansion of Product_{m >= 1} (1 + x^m); number of partitions of n into distinct parts; number of partitions of n into odd parts.

hits: While all prime numbers appear as factors in the Fibonacci numbers, this is not the case with the Lucas numbers. For example, L(n) is never divisible by the following prime numbers < 150: 5, 13, 17, 37, 53, 61, 73, 89, 97, 109, 113, 137, 149 ... See A053028. Conjecture: Three properties can be determined for these prime numbers:
A000032.name: Lucas numbers beginning at 2: L(n) = L(n-1) + L(n-2), L(0) = 2, L(1) = 1.

hits: Conjecture: starting with offset 1 represents the numbers of ordered compositions of n using the signed (++--++...) terms of A001318 starting (1, 2, -5, -7, 12, 15, ...). - _Gary W. Adamson_, Apr 04 2013 (this is true by the pentagonal number theorem, _Joerg Arndt_, Apr 08 2013)
Conjecture: No a(n) has the form x^m with m > 1 and x > 1. - _Zhi-Wei Sun_, Dec 02 2013

Conjecture: Each integer n > 2 different from 6 can be written as a sum of finitely many numbers of the form a(k) + 2 (k > 0) with no summand dividing another. This has been verified for n <= 7140. - _Zhi-Wei Sun_, May 16 2023
A000041.name: a(n) is the number of partitions of n (the partition numbers).

hits: Conjecture: for k > 1, 2^k-1 is (a Mersenne) prime or k = 2^(2^m)+1 (is a Fermat number) if and only if (k-1)^(2^k-2) == 1 (mod (2^k-1)k^2). - _Thomas Ordowski_, Oct 05 2023
Conjecture: for p prime, 2^p-1 is (a Mersenne) prime or p = 2^(2^m)+1 (is a Fermat number) if and only if (p-1)^(2^p-2) == 1 (mod 2^p-1). - _David Barina_, Nov 25 2024
A000043.name: Mersenne exponents: primes p such that 2^p - 1 is prime. Then 2^p - 1 is called a Mersenne prime.

hits: Conjecture: For n > 0, F(n) is the number of all admissible residue classes for which specific finite subsequences of the Collatz 3n + 1 function consists of n+2 terms. This has been verified for 0 < n < 51. For details see Links. - _Mike Winkler_, Oct 03 2014
Conjecture: for all c such that 2-phi <= c < 2*(2-phi) we have F(n) = floor(phi*a(n-1)+c) for n > 2. - _Gerald McGarvey_, Jul 21 2004
A000045.name: Fibonacci numbers: F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2) with F(0) = 0 and F(1) = 1.

hits: Conjecture: Also the number of caliber-n cycles of Zagier-reduced indefinite binary quadratic forms with sum invariant equal to s, where (s-1)/n is an odd integer. - _Barry R. Smith_, Dec 14 2014
A000048.name: Number of n-bead necklaces with beads of 2 colors and primitive period n, when turning over is not allowed but the two colors can be interchanged.

hits: Conjecture: For any integer n >= 0, a(n) is the permanent of the (n+1) X (n+1) matrix with M(j, k) = -floor((j - k - 2)/(n + 1)). This conjecture is inspired by the conjecture of _Zhi-Wei Sun_ in A036968. - _Peter Luschny_, Sep 07 2021
A000051.name: a(n) = 2^n + 1.

hits: Conjecture: the congruence a(n*p^(k+1)) + a(n*p^k) + a(n*p^(k-1)) == 0 (mod p^k) holds for positive integers k and n and for all the primes p listed in A106282. - _Peter Bala_, Dec 28 2022
A000073.name: Tribonacci numbers: a(n) = a(n-1) + a(n-2) + a(n-3) for n >= 3 with a(0) = a(1) = 0 and a(2) = 1.

hits: Conjecture: For any positive integer n, the polynomial Sum_{k=0..n} a(k)*x^k is irreducible over the field of rational numbers. - _Zhi-Wei Sun_, Mar 23 2013

Conjecture: All the rational numbers Sum_{i=j..k} 1/a(i) with 0 < min{2,k} <= j <= k have pairwise distinct fractional parts. - _Zhi-Wei Sun_, Sep 24 2015 - This was proved by an autonomous AI agent, see the Google Deepmind Lean file. - _Ralf Stephan_, May 25 2026
A000108.name: Catalan numbers: C(n) = binomial(2n,n)/(n+1) = (2n)!/(n!(n+1)!).

hits: Conjecture: No a(n) has the form x^m with m > 1 and x > 1. - _Zhi-Wei Sun_, Dec 02 2013
A000110.name: Bell or exponential numbers: number of ways to partition a set of n labeled elements.

hits: Conjecture: Sum_{k>=0} a(k) / exp(k*Pi) = Pi^(1/4)/Gamma(3/4) = A175573. - _Simon Plouffe_, Sep 09 2025
A000122.name: Expansion of Jacobi theta function theta_3(x) = Sum_{m =-oo..oo} x^(m^2) (number of integer solutions to k^2 = n).

hits: Conjecture: Limit_{n ->infinity} (log(n)*a(2n))/(n*a(n)) = c = 1.63... - _Benoit Cloitre_, Jan 26 2003 [The constant c is equal to 2*log(2) = 1.38629436... =A016627. - _Vaclav Kotesovec_, Aug 07 2019]
A000123.name: Number of binary partitions: number of partitions of 2n into powers of 2.

hits: Conjecture. Let S(1)={1} and, for n>1, let S(n) be the smallest set containing x+1 and 2x+1 for each element x in S(n-1). Then a(n) is the number of the elements in S(n). (See A122554 for a sequence defined in this way.) - _John W. Layman_, Nov 21 2007 [edited by _Sela Fried_, Feb 18 2026].
A000126.name: A nonlinear binomial sum.

A000142.name: Factorial numbers: n! = 1*2*3*4*...*n (order of symmetric group S_n, number of permutations of n letters).

hits: Conjecture: a(n) with n > 2 is a perfect power only for n = 4 with a(4) = 3^2. This has been verified for n <= 1000. - _Zhi-Wei Sun_, Jan 09 2025
A000166.name: Subfactorial or rencontres numbers, or derangements: number of permutations of n elements with no fixed points.

hits: Conjecture: a(n) == 2 (mod n^3) iff n is prime. - _Gary Detlefs_, Mar 22 2013
A000172.name: The Franel number a(n) = Sum_{k = 0..n} binomial(n,k)^3.

hits: Conjecture: a(n) = Sum_{k=1..n} A010052(n*k). - _Velin Yanev_, Jul 04 2021
A000188.name: (1) Number of solutions to x^2 == 0 (mod n). (2) Also square root of largest square dividing n. (3) Also max_{ d divides n } gcd(d, n/d).

hits: Conjecture: a(n) is the number of intersection points of n cevians that cut a triangle into the maximum number of pieces (see A007980). - _Anton Zakharov_, May 07 2017
A000212.name: a(n) = floor(n^2/3).

hits: Conjecture: For n > 0, there is always a prime between A000217(n) and A000217(n+1). Sequence A065383 has the first 1000 of these primes. - _Ivan N. Ianakiev_, Mar 11 2013

Conjecture: the sequence is the genus/deficiency of the sinusoidal spirals of index n which are algebraic curves. The value 0 corresponds to the case of the Bernoulli Lemniscate n=2. So the formula conjectured is (n-1)(n-2)/2. - _Wolfgang Tintemann_, Aug 02 2015

Conjecture: Let m be any positive integer. Then, for each n = 1,2,3,... the set {Sum_{k=s..t} 1/k^m: 1 <= s <= t <= n} has cardinality a(n) = n*(n+1)/2; in other words, all the sums Sum_{k=s..t} 1/k^m with 1 <= s <= t are pairwise distinct. (I have checked this conjecture via a computer and found no counterexample.) - _Zhi-Wei Sun_, Sep 09 2015
A000217.name: Triangular numbers: a(n) = binomial(n+1,2) = n*(n+1)/2 = 0 + 1 + 2 + ... + n.

hits: Conjecture: n^2 == 1 (mod a(n)*(a(n)-1)) if and only if n is an odd prime. - _Thomas Ordowski_, Apr 13 2025
A000224.name: Number of squares mod n.

hits: Conjecture: except for a(2)=3, numbers m such that 2^(m+1) - 2^j - 2^k - 1 is composite for all 0 <= j < k <= m. - _Chai Wah Wu_, Sep 08 2021
A000225.name: a(n) = 2^n - 1. (Sometimes called Mersenne numbers, although that name is usually reserved for A001348.)

hits: Conjecture: For n>0, min{k such that there exist subsets A,B of {0,1,2,...,a(n)-1} such that |A|=|B|=k and A+B contains {0,1,2,...,a(n)-1}} = n. - _Michael Chu_, Mar 09 2022
A000290.name: The squares: a(n) = n^2.

hits: Conjecture: a(n) = Sum_{i=0..n} A048994(n, i) * A048993(n+i, n) for n >= 0; proved by Mike Earnest, see link at A354797. - _Werner Schulte_, Jun 19 2022
A000312.name: a(n) = n^n; number of labeled mappings from n points to themselves (endofunctions).

hits: Conjecture: Every integer can be represented as a sum of three generalized square pyramidal numbers. A related conjecture is given in A336205 corresponding to pentagonal case. A stronger version of these conjectures is that every integer can be expressed as a sum of three generalized r-gonal pyramidal numbers for all r >= 3. In here "generalized" means negative indices are included. - _Altug Alkan_, Jul 30 2020
A000330.name: Square pyramidal numbers: a(n) = 0^2 + 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + n^2 = n*(n+1)*(2*n+1)/6.

hits: Conjecture: For n>0, min{k such that there exist subsets A,B of {0,1,2,...,a(n)} such that |A|=|B|=k and A+B={0,1,2,...,2*a(n)}} = 2*n. - _Michael Chu_, Mar 09 2022
A000384.name: Hexagonal numbers: a(n) = n*(2*n-1).

hits: Conjecture. Let S(1)={1} and, for n > 1, let S(n) be the smallest set containing x, 2x and 3x for each element x in S(n-1). Then a(n+2) is the sum of the elements in S(n). (It is easy to prove that the number of elements in S(n) is the n-th triangular number given by A001952.) See A122554 for a sequence defined in this way. - _John W. Layman_, Nov 21 2007; corrected (a(n) to a(n+2) due to offset change) by _Fred Daniel Kline_, Oct 02 2014
A000392.name: Stirling numbers of second kind S(n,3).

hits: Conjecture: for each positive integer k, the sequence defined by a(n) (mod k) is eventually periodic with period dividing phi(k). For example, modulo 13 the sequence becomes [1, 8, 1, 9, 12, 10, 0, 8, 1, 9, 12, 10, 0, ...]; after the initial term 1 this appears to be a periodic sequence of period 6, a divisor of phi(13) = 12. - _Peter Bala_, Dec 11 2021
A000436.name: Generalized Euler numbers c(3,n).

hits: Conjecture: a(n) with n >= 0 can never be a perfect power. Also, the sequence (a(n+1)/a(n))_{n>=0} is strictly decreasing (to the limit 1). - _Zhi-Wei Sun_, Dec 27 2024
Conjecture: Sum_{k>=-1} a(k) / exp(k*Pi) = 66^3 = 287496. - _Simon Plouffe_, Apr 01 2026
A000521.name: Coefficients of modular function j as power series in q = e^(2 Pi i t). Another name is the elliptic modular invariant J(tau).

hits: Conjecture: a(n+3) = Sum_{0 <= k, L, m <= n; k + L + m <= n} k*L*m. - _Ralf Stephan_, May 06 2005
A000579.name: Figurate numbers or binomial coefficients C(n,6).

hits: Conjecture: taking the sequence modulo an integer k gives an eventually purely periodic sequence with period dividing phi(k). For example, the sequence taken modulo 9 begins [1, 1, 4, 1, 7, 4, 1, 7, 4, 1, 7, ...] with an apparent period [4, 1, 7] of length 3 = phi(9)/2 beginning at a(2). - _Peter Bala_, May 08 2023
A000657.name: Median Euler numbers (the middle numbers of Arnold's shuttle triangle).

hits: Conjecture: Let k be a positive integer. The sequence obtained by reducing a(n) modulo k is eventually periodic with the period dividing phi(k) = A000010(k). For example, modulo 16 we obtain the sequence [1, 1, 3, 13, 11, 13, 11, 13, 11, 13, ...], with an apparent period of 2 beginning at a(4). Cf. A354242.
A000670.name: Fubini numbers: number of preferential arrangements of n labeled elements; or number of weak orders on n labeled elements; or number of ordered partitions of [n].

hits: Conjecture: For n > 0 (a(n) + 2^n) is a multiple of (2*n + 1) if and only if (2*n + 1) is a prime number. - _Werner Schulte_, Oct 05 2025
A000680.name: a(n) = (2n)!/2^n.

hits: Conjecture: The sums of distinct powers of k > 2 can be constructed as the following (k-1)-ary rooted tree. For each n the tree grows and a(n) is then the total number of nodes. For n = 1, the root of the tree is added. For n > 1, if n is odd one leaf of depth n-2 grows one child. If n is even all leaves of depth >= (n - 1 - A000225(A001511(n/2))) grow the maximum number of children. An illustration is provided in the links. - _John Tyler Rascoe_, Oct 09 2022
A000695.name: Moser-de Bruijn sequence: sums of distinct powers of 4.

hits: Conjecture: Sum_{k>=0} a(k) / exp(k*Pi) = 2^(1/4) * exp(-Pi/24) = A292828. - _Simon Plouffe_, Sep 09 2025
A000700.name: Expansion of Product_{k>=0} (1 + x^(2k+1)); number of partitions of n into distinct odd parts; number of self-conjugate partitions; number of symmetric Ferrers graphs with n nodes.

hits: Conjecture: : a(n) is divisible by 5 when n is congruent to 2, 3 or 4 modulo 5. (End)
Conjecture: a(25*n + 23) is divisible by 25 (checked for n < 400). [added Dec 26 2025: proved by Chen et al., 2016 - see equation 1.14] - _Peter Bala_, Jan 13 2025
A000712.name: a(n) = number of partitions of n into parts of 2 kinds.

hits: Conjecture: these are numbers m such that Sum_{k=0..m-1} k^phi(m) == phi(m) (mod m), where phi(m) = A000010(m). - _Thomas Ordowski_ and _Giovanni Resta_, Jul 25 2018
A000961.name: Powers of primes. Alternatively, 1 and the prime powers (p^k, p prime, k >= 1).

hits: Conjecture: {a(n)} also gives all j for which A048702(j) = A000217(j); i.e., if we take the a(n)-th triangular number (a(n)^2 + a(n))/2 and multiply it by 3, we get a(n)-th even-length binary palindrome A048701(a(n)) concatenated from a(n) and its reverse. E.g., a(4) = 10, which is 1010 in binary; the tenth triangular number is 55, and 55*3 = 165 = 10100101 in binary. - _Antti Karttunen_, circa 1999. (This has been now proved by Paul K. Stockmeyer in his arXiv:1608.08245 paper.) - _Antti Karttunen_, Aug 31 2016

Conjecture: a(n+1) is the number of compositions of n with two kinds of parts, n and n', where the order of the 1 and 1' does not matter. For n=2, a(3) = 5 compositions, enumerated as follows: 2; 2'; 1,1; 1',1 = 1',1; 1',1'. - _Gregory L. Simay_, Sep 02 2017
Conjecture: For n >= 3, a(n) is the second largest natural number whose Collatz orbit has length n+3. (End)
A000975.name: a(2n) = 2*a(2n-1), a(2n+1) = 2*a(2n)+1 (also a(n) is the n-th number without consecutive equal binary digits).

hits: Conjecture: (2/n)*Sum_{k=1..n} (2k+1)*a(k)^2 is an integer for each positive integer n. - _Zhi-Wei Sun_, Nov 16 2017

Conjecture: If p is a prime of the form 6m+1 (A002476), then a(p-2) is divisible by p. Currently, no counterexample exists for p < 10^7. Personal communication from _Robert Gerbicz_: mod such p this is equivalent to A066796 with comment: "Every A066796(n) from A066796((p-1)/2) to A066796(p-1) is divisible by prime p of form 6m+1". - _Serge Batalov_, Feb 08 2022
A001006.name: Motzkin numbers: number of ways of drawing any number of nonintersecting chords joining n (labeled) points on a circle.

hits: Conjecture: for nonzero m, H(n) = (1/m)*Sum_{k = 1..n} ((-1)^(k+1)/k) * binomial(m*k,k)*binomial(n+(m-1)*k,n-k). The case m = 1 is well-known; the case m = 2 is given above by Detlefs (dated Apr 13 2013). - _Peter Bala_, Mar 04 2022
A001008.name: a(n) = numerator of harmonic number H(n) = Sum_{i=1..n} 1/i.

A001076.name: Denominators of continued fraction convergents to sqrt(5).

hits: Conjecture: sequence contains infinitely many pairs of twin primes. - _Benoit Cloitre_, May 08 2003

Conjecture: for a prime p > 5, p has primitive root 2 iff p == +-3 (mod 8) divides 2^k + 3 for some k < p - 1 and divides 2^m + 5 for some m < p - 1. It seems that all primes of the form 2^k + 3 for k <> 2 (A057732) have primitive root 2. - _Thomas Ordowski_, Nov 27 2023
A001122.name: Primes with primitive root 2.

hits: Conjecture: For each k = 2,3,..., all the rational numbers sigma_k(n)/n^k = Sum_{d|n} 1/d^k (n = 1,2,3,...) have pairwise distinct fractional parts. - _Zhi-Wei Sun_, Oct 15 2015
Conjecture: a(n) = sigma(n^2*rad(n))/sigma(rad(n)), where sigma = A000203 and rad = A007947. - _Velin Yanev_, Aug 20 2017
A001157.name: a(n) = sigma_2(n): sum of squares of divisors of n.

hits: a(n) = 2 for n == 0, 3, 7, 8, 12, 15 (mod 20). a(p^e) = 1 if primes p == 11, 19 (mod 20); 4 if p == 13, 17 (mod 20). Conjecture: 1/6 of the primes congruent to 1 or 9 mod 40 satisfy a(p^e) = 1, 2/3 of them satisfy a(p^e) = 2 and 1/6 of them satisfy a(p^e) = 4; also, 1/2 of the primes congruent to 21 or 29 mod 40 satisfy a(p^e) = 1 and 1/2 of them satisfy a(p^e) = 4. (End)
A001176.name: Number of zeros in fundamental period of Fibonacci numbers mod n.

hits: Conjecture: Sum_{d|n} phi(d)*a(d) = A232656(n). - _Logan J. Kleinwaks_, Oct 28 2017
A001177.name: Fibonacci entry points: a(n) = least k >= 1 such that n divides Fibonacci number F_k (=A000045(k)).

hits: Conjecture: an integer n > 1 such that n^2 divides 2^(n-1)-1 must be a Wieferich prime. - _Thomas Ordowski_, Dec 21 2016
A001220.name: Wieferich primes: primes p such that p^2 divides 2^(p-1) - 1.

hits: Conjecture: Let f(n) = (x+y)^a(n), and g(n) = x^a(n), and h(n) = (x+y)^A046660(n) * y^A001221(n) with x, y complex numbers and 0^0 = 1. Then f(n) = Sum_{d|n} g(d)*h(n/d). This is proved for x = 1-y (see Dressler and van de Lune link). - _Werner Schulte_, Feb 10 2018
A001222.name: Number of prime divisors of n counted with multiplicity (also called big omega of n, bigomega(n) or Omega(n)).

hits: Conjecture: a(n)/n ~ (log(n)/log(log(n)))*(1-(M/log(log(n)))) as n -> oo, where M is Mertens's constant (A077761). - _Alain Rocchelli_, Feb 02 2025
A001358.name: Semiprimes (or biprimes): products of two primes.

hits: Conjecture: For any integers n >= m > 0, there are infinitely many integers b > a(n) such that the number Sum_{k=m..n} a(k)*b^(n-k) (i.e., (a(m), ..., a(n)) in base b) is prime; moreover, when m = 1 there is such an integer b < (n+6)^2. - _Zhi-Wei Sun_, Mar 26 2013

Conjecture: a(n)^(1/n) is a strictly decreasing function of n. Namely a(n+1)^(1/(n+1)) < a(n)^(1/n) for all n. This conjecture is true for all a(n) <= 1121784847637957. - _Jahangeer Kholdi_ and _Farideh Firoozbakht_, Nov 21 2014

Conjecture: Half of the twin prime pairs can be expressed as 8n + M where M > 8n and each value of M is a distinct composite integer with no more than two prime factors. For example, when n=1, M=21 as 8 + 21 = 29, the lesser of a twin prime pair. - _Martin Michael Musatov_, Dec 14 2017
A001359.name: Lesser of twin primes.

hits: Conjecture: barring the 0+2, 0+4, 0+8, 0+16, ... sequence, the sum of 2 distinct terms in this sequence is never a power of 2. - _J. Lowell_, Jan 14 2022
A001481.name: Numbers that are the sum of 2 squares.

hits: As A000005(n) equals the number of even divisors of 2n and A001227(n) = A001227(2n), the formula A001511(n) = A000005(n)/A001227(n) might be read as "The number of even divisors of 2n is always divisible by the number of odd divisors of 2n" (where number of divisors means sum of zeroth powers of divisors). Conjecture: For any nonnegative integer k, the sum of the k-th powers of even divisors of n is always divisible by the sum of the k-th powers of odd divisors of n. - _Ivan N. Ianakiev_, Jul 06 2019
A001511.name: The ruler function: exponent of the highest power of 2 dividing 2n. Equivalently, the 2-adic valuation of 2n.

hits: Starting with 7, the terms end with 7,47,07,47,07,..., of the form 8a+7 where a = 0,1,55,121771,... Conjecture: Every a is squarefree, every other a is divisible by 55, the a's are a subset of A046194, the heptagonal triangular numbers (the first, 2nd, 3rd, 6th, 11th, ?, ... terms). - _Gerald McGarvey_, Aug 08 2004
A001566.name: a(0) = 3; thereafter, a(n) = a(n-1)^2 - 2.

hits: Conjecture: Every harmonic number is practical (A005153). I've verified this refinement of Ore's conjecture for all terms less than 10^14. - _Jaycob Coleman_, Oct 12 2013
Conjecture: All terms > 1 are Zumkeller numbers (A083207). Verified for all n <= 50. - _Ivan N. Ianakiev_, Nov 22 2017
Conjecture: all terms > 1 have a Mersenne prime as a factor. - _Ivan Borysiuk_, Jan 28 2024
A001599.name: Harmonic or Ore numbers: numbers k such that the harmonic mean of the divisors of k is an integer.

hits: Conjecture: a(n) = Sum_{k=2^n..2^(n+1)-1} A178244(k). - _Mikhail Kurkov_, Feb 20 2021
A001700.name: a(n) = binomial(2*n+1, n+1): number of ways to put n+1 indistinguishable balls into n+1 distinguishable boxes = number of (n+1)-st degree monomials in n+1 variables = number of monotone maps from 1..n+1 to 1..n+1.

hits: Conjecture: For n > 2, a(n-3) is the absolute value of the coefficient of the term [x^(n-2)] in the characteristic polynomial of an n X n square matrix M(n) defined as the n-th principal submatrix of the array A010751 whose general element is given by M[i,j] = floor((j - i + 1)/2). - _Stefano Spezia_, Jan 12 2022
A001752.name: Expansion of 1/((1+x)*(1-x)^5).

A001917.name: a(n) = (p-1)/x, where p = prime(n) and x = ord(2,p), the smallest positive integer such that 2^x == 1 (mod p).

hits: Conjecture: a(n+1) == a(n) (mod 3^(n+r+2)) for n >= r.
A002000.name: a(n+1) = a(n)*(a(n)^2 - 3) with a(0) = 7.

hits: Conjecture: Let k be a positive integer. The sequence obtained by reducing a(n) modulo k is eventually periodic with the period dividing phi(k) = A000010(k). For example, modulo 9 we obtain the sequence [0, 1, 5, 7, 5, 1, 5, 4, 5, 7, 5, 1, 5, 4, 5, 7, 5, 1, 5, 4, 5, 7, 5, ...], with an apparent period of 6 = phi(9) beginning at a(5). - _Peter Bala_, Aug 03 2023
A002050.name: Number of simplices in barycentric subdivision of n-simplex.

hits: Conjecture: taking the sequence modulo an integer k gives an eventually purely periodic sequence with period dividing phi(k). For example, the sequence taken modulo 10 begins [1, 1, 4, 4, 6, 6, 4, 4, 6, 6, 4, 4, 6, 6, ...] with an apparent period [4, 4, 6, 6] of length 4 = phi(10) beginning at a(3). - _Peter Bala_, May 08 2023
A002105.name: Reduced tangent numbers: 2^n*(2^{2n} - 1)*|B_{2n}|/n, where B_n = Bernoulli numbers.

hits: Conjecture: for k >= 0 and r even with r - 1 <= k, the series Sum_{n >= 1} (-1)^n * (d/dn)^r (P(n,k)) / (P(n,k)^2  = A(r,k)*log(2) + B(r,k), where A(r,k) and B(r,k) are both rational numbers. (End)
A002162.name: Decimal expansion of the natural logarithm of 2.

hits: Conjecture: if p is an odd prime then a((p^3-1)/2) = p * a((p^2-1)/2). Because otherwise a((p^3-1)/2) < p * a((p^2-1)/2) iff a((p^3-1)/2) = a((p-1)/2) for a prime p. Equivalently p^3 divides 2^(p-1)-1, but no such prime p is known. - _Thomas Ordowski_, Feb 10 2014
A002326.name: Multiplicative order of 2 mod 2n+1.

hits: Conjecture: An integer n > 3 is prime if and only if a(n) == 1 (mod n^2). We have verified this for n up to 8*10^5, and proved that a(p) == 1 (mod p^2) for any prime p > 3 (cf. A277640). - _Zhi-Wei Sun_, Nov 30 2016
Conjecture: The stronger congruences a(n*p^k) == a(n*p^(k-1)) (mod p^(2*k)) hold for all prime p >= 5 and positive integers n and k. (End)
A002426.name: Central trinomial coefficients: largest coefficient of (1 + x + x^2)^n.

hits: Imagine a torus having regular polygonal cross-section of m sides. Now, break the torus and twist the free ends, preserving rotational symmetry, then reattach the ends. Now, count the independent, closed paths on the surface of the resulting torus, where a path is "closed" if and only if it returns to its starting point after a finite number of times around the surface of the torus. Conjecture: this number is always gcd(m,n). NOTE: This figure constitutes a group with m and n the binary arguments and gcd(m,n) the resulting value. hits: Conjecture: there are no finite cycles of any length. My grounds for this conjecture: any finite cycle in this sequence, if such cycles exist at all, must have at least one member that occurs somewhere in A285319, the terms that seem already to be quite rare. Moreover, any such a number n should satisfy in addition to A019565(n) < n also that A048675^{k}(n) is squarefree, not just for k=0, 1 but for all k >= 0. As there is on average a probability of only 6/(Pi^2) = 0.6079... that any further term encountered on the trajectory of A048675 is squarefree, the total chance that all of them would be squarefree (which is required from the elements of A019565-cycles) is soon minuscule, especially as A048675 is not very tightly bounded (many trajectories seem to skyrocket, at least initially). I am also assuming that usually there is no significant correlation between the binary expansions of n and A048675(n) (apart from their least significant bits), or, for that matter, between their prime factorizations.

hits: Conjecture: This is a permutation of the positive integers, with primes in order. Each prime p generates a trajectory T(p), dominated by multiples of p, see graph. Typically T(prime(k)) is initiated following the earliest term divisible by prime(k). Some trajectories are more prominent in the graph than others e.g. T(7),T(11),T(13) extend from p = prime(k) to prime(k+1)*prime(k). Others, e.g. T(3) terminate earlier but include prime(k)^2, whilst some do not reach as far as prime(k)^2 (T(5) has just two terms). Thus three categories of prime trajectory can be distinguished in the graph (respectively "full", "medium" and "small"). The graph resembles an inclined comb whose teeth correspond to full and medium trajectories; see Example.
